title: Part 3, Chapter 3
paragraphs: "He's doing well, quite well!" Zossimov announced cheerfully as they came in.

He had arrived ten minutes earlier and was sitting in his usual spot on the sofa. Raskolnikov sat in the opposite corner, fully dressed and carefully washed and combed for the first time in a while. The room was immediately crowded, but Nastasya managed to follow the visitors in and stayed to listen.

Compared with the day before, Raskolnikov really was almost well, but he was still pale, listless, and gloomy. He looked like a wounded man or someone who had endured terrible physical suffering. His brows were knitted, his lips compressed, his eyes feverish. He spoke little and reluctantly, as though fulfilling a duty, and there was a restlessness in his movements.

All he needed was a sling on his arm or a bandage on his finger to complete the picture of a man with a painful abscess or a broken arm. His pale, gloomy face brightened for a moment when his mother and sister entered, but this only gave it a look of more intense suffering instead of listless dejection. The light quickly faded, but the suffering remained. Zossimov, watching and studying his patient with all the enthusiasm of a young doctor just starting out, noticed no joy at the arrival of his mother and sister, only a kind of bitter, hidden determination to endure another hour or two of unavoidable torture. He later observed that almost every word of the conversation seemed to touch some sore spot and irritate it. At the same time he marvelled at the patient's ability to control himself and hide his feelings, when just the day before he had flown into a frenzy like a madman at the slightest word.

"Yes, I can see myself now that I'm almost well," said Raskolnikov, kissing his mother and sister in welcome, which made Pulcheria Alexandrovna beam at once. "And I don't say this the way I did yesterday," he added, addressing Razumihin with a friendly squeeze of his hand.

"Yes, I'm quite surprised at him today," Zossimov began, clearly delighted by the ladies' entrance, since he hadn't managed to keep up a conversation with his patient for ten minutes. "In another three or four days, if he goes on like this, he'll be just as he was a month or two ago, perhaps even three. This has been building up for a long time, hasn't it? Admit it now, it's perhaps been partly your own fault?" he added with a tentative smile, as though still afraid of irritating him.
"Quite possibly," answered Raskolnikov coldly.

"I would also say," Zossimov continued eagerly, "that your complete recovery depends entirely on you. Now that we can talk, I want to impress upon you that it's essential to address the root causes of your condition. If you do, you'll recover; if not, things will only get worse. I don't know what those causes are, but you must. You're an intelligent man and must have observed yourself. I believe the onset of your illness coincides with your leaving the university. You shouldn't be idle. Work and a clear purpose might do you a great deal of good."
"Yes, yes, you're absolutely right. I'll go back to the university right away, and then everything will be fine..."

Zossimov, who had begun his sage advice partly to impress the ladies, was rather thrown off when he noticed unmistakable mockery on his patient's face. But it lasted only an instant. Pulcheria Alexandrovna immediately began thanking Zossimov, especially for his visit to their lodging the previous night.
"What! He visited you last night?" Raskolnikov asked, as though startled. "So you didn't sleep either after your journey."
"Oh, Rodya, that was only until two o'clock. Dounia and I never go to bed before two at home."

"I don't know how to thank him either," Raskolnikov went on, suddenly frowning and looking down. "Setting aside the question of payment—forgive me for bringing it up"—he turned to Zossimov—"I really don't understand what I've done to deserve such special attention from you. I simply don't understand it, and it weighs on me, precisely because I don't understand. I'm telling you frankly."

"Don't be irritated," Zossimov said, forcing a laugh. "Think of yourself as my first patient. We young doctors love our first patients as if they were our own children, and some practically fall in love with them. And I'm not exactly drowning in patients."
"I'm not even talking about him," Raskolnikov added, pointing to Razumihin, "though he's had nothing from me but insults and trouble."
"What nonsense! You're in a sentimental mood today, are you?" Razumihin shouted.

If he'd been more perceptive, he would have seen that there was no trace of sentimentality in Raskolnikov, but something quite the opposite. Avdotya Romanovna noticed it, though. She was watching her brother intently and uneasily.

"As for you, mother, I don't dare speak," he continued, as though reciting a lesson he'd memorized. "It's only today that I've begun to realize how worried you must have been yesterday, waiting for me to come back."

As he said this, he suddenly held out his hand to his sister, smiling wordlessly. But in that smile there was a flash of real, genuine feeling. Dounia caught it at once and warmly pressed his hand, overjoyed and grateful. It was the first time he had reached out to her since their argument the day before. Their mother's face lit up with radiant happiness at this silent reconciliation. "Yes, that's what I love about him," Razumihin muttered to himself, exaggerating as usual, with a vigorous turn in his chair. "He has these moments."

"And how well he does everything," the mother thought to herself. "What generous impulses, and how simply, how delicately he resolved the misunderstanding with his sister—just by holding out his hand at the right moment and looking at her like that. And what fine eyes, and how handsome his whole face is! He's even better looking than Dounia. But, heavens, what a suit—how terribly he's dressed! Vasya, the errand boy at Afanasy Ivanitch's shop, is better dressed! I could throw myself on him and hug him, cry over him—but I'm afraid. Oh dear, he's so strange! He's speaking kindly, but I'm afraid! What am I afraid of?"

"Oh, Rodya, you wouldn't believe," she began suddenly, rushing to respond, "how unhappy Dounia and I were yesterday! Now that it's all over and we're happy again—I can tell you. We came here practically straight from the train to see you, and that woman—oh, here she is! Good morning, Nastasya! She told us right away that you were delirious with fever and had run away from the doctor, and they were searching the streets for you. You can't imagine how we felt! I kept thinking of the tragic fate of Lieutenant Potanchikov, a friend of your father's—you can't remember him, Rodya—who ran out the same way in a high fever and fell into the well in the courtyard, and they couldn't pull him out till the next day. Of course we were exaggerating. We were about to rush off and find Pyotr Petrovitch to ask for his help, because we were alone, utterly alone," she said plaintively, then stopped short, suddenly remembering that it was still somewhat dangerous to mention Pyotr Petrovitch, even though "we're quite happy again."
"Yes, yes. Of course that's very upsetting," Raskolnikov muttered in reply, but with such a distracted and inattentive air that Dounia stared at him in puzzlement.
"What else was I going to say?" He tried to remember. "Oh, yes—mother, and you too, Dounia, please don't think I wasn't planning to come see you today and was just waiting for you to come first."
"What are you saying, Rodya?" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna, equally surprised.
"Is he answering us out of duty?" Dounia wondered. "Being reconciled and asking forgiveness like he's performing a ritual or reciting a lesson?"
"I only just woke up and wanted to come to you, but I was held up because of my clothes. I forgot yesterday to ask her—Nastasya—to wash out the blood. I've only just gotten dressed."
"Blood! What blood?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked in alarm.
"Oh, it's nothing—don't worry. When I was wandering around yesterday, a bit delirious, I came across a man who'd been run over—a clerk..."
"Delirious? But you remember everything!" Razumihin interrupted.
"That's true," Raskolnikov answered with particular care. "I remember everything down to the smallest detail, yet why I did that, why I went there and said what I said—I can't explain clearly now."

"A familiar phenomenon," Zossimov put in. "Actions are sometimes performed in a masterful and most cunning way, while the direction of those actions is deranged, driven by various morbid impulses—rather like a dream."
"Perhaps it's a good thing he thinks I'm practically mad," Raskolnikov thought.
"But perfectly healthy people act the same way too," Dounia observed, glancing uneasily at Zossimov.

"There's some truth in that," the doctor replied. "In that sense, we're all not infrequently a bit like madmen, but with the slight difference that the truly deranged are somewhat more so. We need to draw a line somewhere. A truly normal person barely exists. Among dozens—perhaps hundreds of thousands—you'd hardly find one."
At the word "madman," carelessly dropped by Zossimov while chattering about his favourite subject, everyone frowned.
Raskolnikov sat as if paying no attention, sunk in thought with a strange smile on his pale lips. He was still turning something over in his mind.
"Well, what about the man who was run over? I interrupted you!" Razumihin cried hastily.

"What?" Raskolnikov seemed to wake up. "Oh, I got splattered with blood helping carry him to his lodging. By the way, mother, I did something unforgivable yesterday. I was literally out of my mind. I gave away all the money you sent me to his wife for the funeral. She's a widow now, consumptive, a pitiful creature, three small children, starving, nothing in the house. There's a daughter too. Perhaps you would have given it yourself if you'd seen them. But I had no right to do it, I admit, especially knowing how much you needed that money yourselves. To help others, one must first have the right to do so, otherwise—'Die, dogs, if you're not content!' That's right, isn't it, Dounia?"
"No, it's not," Dounia answered firmly.

"Bah! You too have your ideals," he muttered, looking at her almost with hatred and smiling sarcastically. "I should have thought of that. Well, it's admirable, and better for you. If you reach a certain line and don't cross it, you'll be unhappy; but if you cross it, perhaps you'll be unhappier still. But all that's nonsense," he added irritably, annoyed at having been carried away. "I only meant to say that I beg your forgiveness, mother," he concluded shortly and abruptly.
"That's enough, Rodya. I'm sure everything you do is right," his mother said, delighted.
"Don't be too sure," he answered, twisting his mouth into a smile.
A silence followed. There was a certain awkwardness in everything—the conversation, the silence, the reconciliation, the forgiveness—and everyone felt it.
"It's as though they're afraid of me," Raskolnikov thought, glancing sideways at his mother and sister. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was indeed growing more timid the longer the silence lasted.
"Yet when they weren't here, I seemed to love them so much," flashed through his mind.
"Do you know, Rodya, Marfa Petrovna is dead," Pulcheria Alexandrovna suddenly blurted out.
"What Marfa Petrovna?"
"For heaven's sake—Marfa Petrovna Svidrigaïlov! I wrote you so much about her."
"A-ah! Yes, I remember. So she's dead? Really?" He roused himself suddenly, as if waking up. "What did she die of?"

"Just imagine, completely suddenly," Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered hurriedly, encouraged by his interest. "On the very day I sent you that letter! Would you believe it—that terrible man seems to have been the cause of her death. They say he beat her dreadfully."
"Were they really on such bad terms?" he asked, turning to his sister.

"Not at all. Quite the contrary, in fact. He was always very patient with her, even considerate. For all seven years of their marriage he gave in to her, too much so in many ways. Then all of a sudden, it seems, he lost his patience."
"So he can't have been that terrible if he kept himself in check for seven years? You seem to be defending him, Dounia."
"No, no, he's a terrible man! I can't imagine anyone more terrible!" Dounia answered, almost shuddering, knitting her brows and sinking into thought.

"It happened in the morning," Pulcheria Alexandrovna continued hurriedly. "Right afterward she ordered the horses harnessed to drive to town immediately after dinner. She always went to town in such cases. She ate a very good dinner, so I'm told..."
"After the beating?"

"That was always her habit. And right after dinner, so as not to be late setting off, she went to the bathhouse. You see, she was taking some kind of bathing treatment. They have a cold spring there, and she used to bathe in it every day. No sooner had she gotten into the water than she had a stroke!"
"I should think so," said Zossimov.
"And was the beating severe?"
"What does that matter!" Dounia put in.
"Hmm! I don't really know why you want to tell us this gossip, mother," said Raskolnikov irritably, as though in spite of himself.
"Oh, my dear, I don't know what else to talk about," Pulcheria Alexandrovna let slip.
"Why, are you all afraid of me?" he asked with a strained smile.
"That's certainly true," said Dounia, looking directly and sternly at her brother. "Mother was crossing herself in terror as she came up the stairs."
His face twisted, as though in a spasm.

"Oh, what are you saying, Dounia! Don't be angry, please, Rodya. Why did you say that, Dounia?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, overwhelmed. "You see, coming here, I dreamed the whole way on the train about how we'd meet, how we'd talk everything over together. And I was so happy I didn't notice the journey! But what am I saying? I'm happy now, simply seeing you, Rodya."
"Hush, mother," he muttered in confusion, not looking at her but pressing her hand. "We'll have time to talk freely about everything."

As he said this, he was suddenly overwhelmed by confusion and turned pale. Again that terrible sensation he'd come to know so well lately passed through his soul with a deathly chill. Again it became suddenly, piercingly clear that he had just told a dreadful lie—that he would never be able to speak freely about everything, never again be able to truly speak to anyone about anything. The anguish of this realization was so acute that for a moment he nearly lost himself. He stood up from his seat and, without looking at anyone, walked toward the door.
"What are you doing?" Razumihin cried, grabbing his arm.
He sat down again and began looking around in silence. Everyone stared at him in bewilderment.

"What's wrong with you all—why so glum?" he burst out suddenly and quite unexpectedly. "Say something! What's the point of sitting here like this? Come on, talk! Let's have a conversation. We finally get together and sit in silence. Come on, anything!"
"Thank God! I was afraid the same thing as yesterday was starting again," said Pulcheria Alexandrovna, crossing herself.
"What's the matter, Rodya?" Avdotya Romanovna asked suspiciously.
"Oh, nothing! I just remembered something," he answered, and suddenly laughed.

"Well, if you remembered something, that's fine! I was beginning to think..." Zossimov muttered, getting up from the sofa. "It's time I was off. I'll look in again perhaps, if I can." He bowed and went out.
"What an excellent man!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna observed.

"Yes, excellent, splendid, well-educated, intelligent," Raskolnikov began, suddenly speaking with surprising speed and a liveliness he hadn't shown before. "I can't remember where I met him before my illness. I think I did meet him somewhere. And this one is a good man, too," he nodded at Razumihin. "Do you like him, Dounia?" he asked her, and for some unknown reason burst out laughing.
"Very much," answered Dounia.
"Ugh, what a pig you are!" Razumihin protested, blushing crimson with embarrassment as he got up from his chair. Pulcheria Alexandrovna smiled faintly, but Raskolnikov laughed out loud.
"Where are you going?"
"I have to go."

"You don't have to at all. Stay. Zossimov's gone, so you have to stay. Don't go. What time is it? Is it twelve? What a pretty watch you've got, Dounia. Why are you all silent again? I'm doing all the talking."
"It was a present from Marfa Petrovna," answered Dounia.
"And quite an expensive one!" added Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
"Ah! It's a big one, hardly ladylike."
"I like that sort," said Dounia.
"So it's not a present from her fiancé," Razumihin thought, unreasonably delighted.
"I thought it was Luzhin's present," Raskolnikov observed.
"No, he hasn't given Dounia any presents yet."
"Ah! And do you remember, mother, I was in love and wanted to get married?" he said suddenly, looking at his mother, who was startled by the abrupt change of subject and the way he spoke of it.
"Oh, yes, my dear."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna exchanged glances with Dounia and Razumihin.

"Hmm, yes. What can I tell you? I don't even remember much. She was such a sickly girl," he went on, growing dreamy and looking down. "Quite an invalid. She liked giving alms to the poor and was always dreaming of entering a convent, and once she burst into tears when she started telling me about it. Yes, yes, I remember very well. She was an ugly little thing. I really don't know what attracted me to her—I think it was because she was always ill. If she'd been lame or hunchbacked, I think I'd have liked her even more," he smiled dreamily. "Yes, it was a sort of spring delirium."
"No, it wasn't only spring delirium," said Dounia with warm feeling.

He fixed a strained, intent look on his sister, but either didn't hear or didn't understand her words. Then, completely lost in thought, he got up, went to his mother, kissed her, went back to his place, and sat down.
"You still love her?" said Pulcheria Alexandrovna, touched.

"Her? Now? Oh, yes. You're asking about her? No, that's all in another world now, and so long ago. And indeed everything happening here seems somehow far away." He looked at them attentively. "You, for instance, I seem to be looking at you from a thousand miles away. But God knows why we're even talking about this! And what's the use of asking?" he added with annoyance, and fell into pensive silence, biting his nails.

"What a wretched room you have, Rodya! It's like a tomb," Pulcheria Alexandrovna said suddenly, breaking the oppressive silence. "I'm sure it's at least half because of this room that you've become so melancholy."
"My room," he answered absently. "Yes, the room had a lot to do with it. I thought that too. But if only you knew, mother, what a strange thing you just said," he added with a peculiar laugh.

A little more and the situation—his mother and sister beside him after three years apart, their intimate tone of conversation in the face of the utter impossibility of truly speaking about anything—would have been more than he could bear. But there was one urgent matter that had to be settled one way or another that day. He'd decided that when he woke up. Now he was glad to remember it as a way out.

"Listen, Dounia," he began gravely and drily, "of course I apologize for yesterday, but I feel it's my duty to tell you again that I'm not backing down from my main point. It's either me or Luzhin. If I'm a scoundrel, you shouldn't be one too. One of us is enough. If you marry Luzhin, I will immediately stop considering you my sister."
"Rodya, Rodya! It's the same as yesterday all over again," Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried mournfully. "And why do you call yourself a scoundrel? I can't bear it. You said the same thing yesterday."

"Brother," Dounia answered firmly and with the same dryness. "You're making a mistake about all this. I thought it over during the night and found where the mistake lies. It's all because you seem to think I'm sacrificing myself for someone. That's not the case at all. I'm simply marrying for my own sake, because things are hard for me. Of course, I'll be glad if I can also be useful to my family. But that's not the main reason for my decision."

"She's lying," he thought, biting his nails vindictively. "Proud creature! She won't admit she wants to do it out of charity! Too proud! Oh, vile natures! They even love as though they hate. Oh, how I hate them all!"

"In fact," Dounia continued, "I'm marrying Pyotr Petrovitch because of two evils I'm choosing the lesser. I intend to fulfill honestly everything he expects of me, so I'm not deceiving him. Why did you just smile?" She flushed too, and there was a flash of anger in her eyes.
"Everything?" he asked with a malicious grin.

"Within certain limits. Both the manner and form of Pyotr Petrovitch's courtship showed me at once what he wanted. He may think too well of himself, but I hope he values me too. Why are you laughing again?"

"And why are you blushing again? You're lying, sister. You're deliberately lying, out of sheer feminine stubbornness, just to hold your own against me. You can't possibly respect Luzhin. I've seen him and spoken with him. So you're selling yourself for money, and in any case you're acting basely. I'm glad at least that you can still blush about it."

"That's not true! I'm not lying!" cried Dounia, losing her composure. "I wouldn't marry him if I weren't convinced he respects me and thinks highly of me. I wouldn't marry him if I weren't firmly certain I can respect him. Fortunately, I'll have convincing proof of that today, and such a marriage isn't a vile thing, as you say! And even if you were right, even if I really had resolved on something vile, isn't it heartless of you to speak to me like that? Why do you demand heroism from me that perhaps you don't have either? That's tyranny! If I ruin anyone, it's only myself. I'm not committing murder! Why are you looking at me like that? Why are you so pale? Rodya, darling, what's wrong?"
"Good heavens! You've made him faint!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.

"No, no, it's nothing. Just a bit of dizziness—not fainting. You have fainting on the brain. Hmm, yes, what was I saying? Oh, yes. How exactly will you get this convincing proof today that you can respect him and that he values you, as you said? I believe you said today?"
"Mother, show Rodya Pyotr Petrovitch's letter," said Dounia.
With trembling hands, Pulcheria Alexandrovna gave him the letter. He took it with great interest, but before opening it, he suddenly looked at Dounia with something like wonder.
"Strange," he said slowly, as though struck by a new idea. "What am I making such a fuss about? What's it all about? Marry whoever you want!"

He seemed to be saying this to himself, but he said it aloud, and looked at his sister for some time, as if puzzled. He finally opened the letter, still with that expression of strange wonder, and read it through twice, slowly and attentively. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was visibly anxious, and indeed everyone expected something significant.

"What surprises me," he began after a short pause, handing the letter back to his mother without addressing anyone in particular, "is that he's a businessman, a lawyer, and his conversation is quite pretentious, yet he writes such an uneducated letter."
They all started. They had expected something quite different.
"But they all write like that, you know," Razumihin observed abruptly.
"You've read it?"
"Yes."
"We showed him, Rodya. We consulted him just now," Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, embarrassed.
"That's just legal jargon," Razumihin put in. "Legal documents are still written that way."
"Legal? Yes, it's exactly that—business language. Not terribly uneducated, not quite educated—business language!"
"Pyotr Petrovitch makes no secret of having had a modest education. He's even proud of being self-made," Avdotya Romanovna observed, somewhat offended by her brother's tone.

"Well, if he's proud of it, he has reason to be—I don't deny it. You seem offended, sister, that I'm making such a trivial criticism of the letter, and you think I'm bringing up petty things just to annoy you. It's quite the opposite. Something about the style struck me that's very relevant to our situation. There's one phrase—'blame yourselves'—put very significantly and plainly, and there's also a threat to leave at once if I'm present. That threat to leave amounts to a threat to abandon you both if you don't obey, to abandon you now, after summoning you to Petersburg. Well, tell me: can you take offense at such a phrase from Luzhin the way you would if it came from him"—he pointed to Razumihin—"or Zossimov, or any of us?"

"N-no," answered Dounia, more animatedly. "I could see clearly that it was too crudely expressed, and that perhaps he simply lacks skill with words. That's a fair observation, brother. I really didn't expect it."

"It's written in legal style and comes across as harsher than he perhaps intended. But I need to disillusion you a bit. There's one passage in the letter, a slander against me, and a rather contemptible one. I gave the money last night to the widow, a woman dying of consumption, crushed by hardship—not 'on the pretext of the funeral,' as he writes, but simply to pay for the funeral. I gave it not to the daughter—a young woman, as he describes, of notorious behaviour, whom I saw for the first time last night—but to the widow. In all this I see an eagerness to slander me and create a rift between us. Again it's expressed in legal language—that is, with too obvious an intent and too naïve an eagerness. He's an intelligent man, but intelligence alone isn't enough to act wisely. It all reveals the man, and I don't think he has much genuine respect for you. I tell you this simply as a warning, because I sincerely wish you well."
Dounia did not reply. Her decision had already been made. She was only waiting for the evening.
"Then what is your decision, Rodya?" asked Pulcheria Alexandrovna, more uneasy than ever at the sudden new business-like tone of his words.
"What decision?"
"You see, Pyotr Petrovitch writes that you shouldn't be with us this evening, and that he'll leave if you come. So will you come?"

"That, of course, is not for me to decide, but for you first—if such a demand doesn't offend you—and secondly, for Dounia, if she's not offended either. I'll do whatever you think best," he added drily.
"Dounia has already decided, and I agree completely," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hastened to say.
"I've decided to ask you, Rodya, to make a point of being with us at this meeting," said Dounia. "Will you come?"
"Yes."
"I'd like to ask you too, to join us at eight," she said, turning to Razumihin. "Mother, I'm inviting him as well."

"Quite right, Dounia. Well, since you've decided," Pulcheria Alexandrovna added, "so be it. I'll feel easier myself. I don't like hiding things and deceiving people. Better to have it all out in the open. Let Pyotr Petrovitch be angry or not!"
